lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Fall 2022. A room full of students, laptops open, and one question hanging over everything: is using Copilot cheating?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Ha, I remember that energy. What did they do about it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Cédille, the ÉTS consulting club, invited GitHub and Arctiq to talk about Copilot and the AI tooling around it. The idea was to hear it from people who actually ship the product instead of relying on rumours.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Whether Copilot was allowed on internships, whether it helped with data labs, or whether it would get you failed on code review. Practical stuff.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what did the demo show?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Copilot Chat, for explanations and refactors in the editor, not just tab completions. And a slash command called createNotebook that bootstraps a Jupyter notebook from code already in a repo.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That one got the room, I'd guess.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It was the crowd reaction moment. Point Chat at a module, ask for a notebook that demonstrates it, get a first draft. Antoine's careful to say it's not magic, you still verify paths and versions.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Privacy, meaning what leaves the machine. Licensing of generated code. And whether it works offline. It doesn't, so plan demos with Wi-Fi.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Follow your course policy and understand every line you submit. Run the code, read the diff. And the best first win is explaining unfamiliar code and generating test scaffolding, not writing your whole lab.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So Copilot as a fast draft.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, an accelerator, not an author. Review still belongs to the human who commits.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The full write-up has the photos from the session.
